1980:
"Bona fide" means genuine, real, and authentic — exactly what something or someone claims to be. When you call something bona fide, you are saying: this is the real thing, not a fake, not an imitation, not a trick.

Think of it this way: if you bought a painting that was signed "Picasso," a bona fide Picasso would mean it was truly painted by Picasso himself — not a copy, not a forgery, not a painting that merely looks like his style.

The most important idea inside "bona fide" is the absence of deception. It doesn't just mean "real" in a casual sense. It means real in a way that can be trusted and verified. There is no hidden agenda, no fraud, no pretending involved.

This is why the word is often used when someone's legitimacy is being questioned or confirmed. You reach for "bona fide" precisely when you want to settle a doubt — to say: yes, this person or thing is exactly what it appears to be.

This is crucial: "bona fide" is about authenticity, not quality. It does not mean something is good, impressive, or excellent. It only means it is genuine.

  • A bona fide mistake is a real mistake — not an impressive one.
  • A bona fide failure is a true failure — not a noble one.

So if someone says "that was a bona fide disaster," they mean it was a genuine, undeniable disaster — not that the disaster was somehow admirable.
How It Feels in a Sentence

"Bona fide" carries a slightly emphatic, confirmatory energy. Saying "she's a bona fide expert" feels stronger than simply saying "she's a real expert." It has a sense of I am vouching for this — there is no question about it. It pushes back against doubt with confidence.

People:

  • "He is a bona fide scientist" — He genuinely is a scientist. He has the credentials, the training, and the expertise. He isn't just playing one or claiming to be one.
  • "She became a bona fide celebrity overnight" — She is a real, undeniable celebrity now — not a minor or questionable one.

Things and situations:

  • "This is a bona fide emergency" — This is a real emergency, not an exaggeration or a false alarm.
  • "They made a bona fide offer to buy the house" — The offer was sincere and serious, not a casual or dishonest one.
  • "That record is a bona fide classic" — It is genuinely, indisputably a classic — confirmed by time and recognition.

In legal and formal settings:
"Bona fide" is used a lot in law. A bona fide purchaser is someone who bought something honestly — they paid a fair price and had no idea the item was stolen or had any hidden legal problems. Here, the word emphasizes that the person acted with honesty and good faith, without any intent to deceive.
The Difference Between Bona Fide and Similar Words

• Real is simple and neutral. "A real doctor."
  • Genuine emphasizes that something is not a copy or imitation. "A genuine signature."
  • Legitimate emphasizes that something follows the proper rules or standards. "A legitimate business."
  • Bona fide combines elements of all three — it says something is real, not imitated, and can be trusted as exactly what it claims to be. It also carries a slightly more formal, confirmatory weight than the others.

Anything described as bona fide stands in direct contrast to things that are: fake, fraudulent, counterfeit, pretend, phony, or a sham. If a bona fide diamond is the real gemstone, a non-bona fide one is a piece of glass dressed up to look like it.

"Bona fide" naturally appears before nouns like: expert, offer, member, resident, emergency, classic, star, talent, deal, reason, and mistake. You will almost always see it placed directly before the noun it describes.
"Bona fide" means something or someone is completely genuine — truly what it claims to be — with no deception, no fraud, and no imitation involved.
1981:
A bonanza is a sudden, large source of great wealth, profit, or something extremely valuable and desirable. Think of it as a moment or a situation where good things — usually money or resources — flow in much, much more than expected or than usual.

The single most important thing to understand is this: a bonanza is not just "a good thing." It is an overwhelmingly good thing. The scale and abundance are what define it.

Imagine you own a small farm. One year, due to perfect weather, your harvest is ten times bigger than normal. You sell everything and make more money than you've ever made in your life. That harvest is a bonanza.

Now imagine a company releases a product, and it unexpectedly sells millions of copies overnight. That moment is a bonanza for the company.

The word captures that feeling of striking it enormously rich — of abundance arriving in a big, often surprising way.
The Three Key Qualities of a Bonanza

For something to qualify as a bonanza, it typically has these qualities:

1. Great scale or abundance
A bonanza is never small. It involves a large, impressive amount — of money, profit, opportunity, or resources. If something is just "a little extra," it is not a bonanza.

2. A strong sense of good fortune
A bonanza is always a positive thing. It benefits someone. There is no such thing as a "bad bonanza." The word has an inherently cheerful, exciting energy to it.

3. A feeling of windfall or unexpected richness
A bonanza often (though not always) carries a sense of something that came in more generously than expected. It feels like luck, even when it results from hard work — because the scale of reward feels extraordinary.
What a Bonanza Can Refer To

The word is flexible. A bonanza can be:

  • A situation — "The oil discovery was a bonanza for the country."
  • A time period — "Last year was a bonanza year for the film industry."
  • A source of profit or gain — "The new law turned out to be a bonanza for large corporations."
  • An event or occurrence — "The holiday shopping season is a bonanza for retailers."
  • A literal physical discovery (in its original mining sense) — "The miners hit a bonanza deep in the mountain."

Notice how the word can be applied in finance, business, farming, politics, entertainment, and everyday life. Its use is wide.

Bonanza is not a dry or neutral word. It carries enthusiasm and excitement. When you use it, you are not just reporting a fact — you are conveying a sense of wow, that's a lot, that's incredible. Journalists and writers often use it to make headlines more vivid and energetic.

It sits in a slightly informal register, which means it is very common in newspapers, magazines, and everyday speech, but you might avoid it in the most formal academic writing.
Collocations — Words That Naturally Go With "Bonanza"

Here are the most natural and common ways the word appears:

  • a bonanza for [someone] — "The deal was a bonanza for investors."
  • a bonanza of [something] — "A bonanza of opportunities opened up."
  • a bonanza year/season/period — "Farmers are hoping for a bonanza season."
  • strike a bonanza — "The company struck a bonanza with its new product."
  • reap a bonanza — "Early investors reaped a bonanza when the stock soared."
  • an economic/financial bonanza — "Tourism became an economic bonanza for the small town."
  • a windfall bonanza — used when the good fortune is especially sudden and unexpected.
How It Differs From Similar Words

• Windfall — Also means unexpected good fortune, but a windfall is usually a one-time event (like receiving an inheritance). A bonanza can describe an ongoing rich situation, not just a single moment.
  • Jackpot — More specifically tied to gambling and luck; more casual and playful. A bonanza sounds more substantial and weighty.
  • Godsend — Focuses on how desperately welcome something is. A bonanza focuses on the scale of what arrived, not necessarily the need for it.
  • Boom — A boom describes a general period of rapid growth (an economic boom). A bonanza is more specific — it describes a particularly rich, rewarding outcome for someone or something.

• It does not mean just "a good deal" or "a bargain." The scale matters.
  • It does not carry any sense of hardship or negativity. You will never see it used to describe something bad happening to someone.
  • It is not the same as simply "a lot of something." A traffic jam is a lot of cars, but it is not a bonanza. The abundance in a bonanza is always desirable.

A bonanza (noun) is a situation, source, event, or period that brings an exceptionally large amount of wealth, profit, or something greatly valued — often in a way that feels extraordinarily fortunate. It always implies abundance, positivity, and impressive scale.

If you ever see the word and feel unsure, ask yourself: Is someone or something receiving a large, exciting, rewarding flow of something good? If yes — that is a bonanza.
1982: A bond is something that connects, holds, or ties things together — whether those things are people, objects, atoms, or agreements. Think of it as an invisible or visible "link" between two or more things. Every meaning of this word comes back to that central idea of connection and holding.

This is the most everyday meaning. When two people (or a person and an animal) feel a strong sense of closeness, loyalty, or love for each other, that feeling is called a bond.

Examples:

  • The bond between a mother and her child is one of the strongest known to humans.
  • After years of working together through tough times, the soldiers formed an unbreakable bond.
  • A dog often develops a deep bond with its owner.

Think of it as an invisible thread connecting two hearts. You can't see it or touch it, but you can feel it — and it's real. The stronger the shared experiences, trust, and love, the stronger the bond.

A bond can also mean a serious, binding promise — one that you are morally or legally expected to keep. When someone says "my word is my bond," they mean their promise is as solid and trustworthy as a written contract.

Examples:

  • The two business partners shook hands, and for them, that handshake was a bond.
  • He gave his bond that he would return the money within a year.

Here, the "connection" is between a person and their word — they are tied to what they have promised.

In the world of finance and investing, a bond is a type of loan — but one that works in reverse from how most people think of loans.

Here's how it works simply:

  • A government or company needs to borrow a large amount of money.
  • Instead of going to one bank, they borrow from thousands of ordinary people (investors).
  • Each investor buys a "bond" for a fixed price (say, $1,000).
  • The government or company promises to pay the investor regular interest (called a coupon) over a set number of years.
  • At the end of that period (the maturity date), they return the original $1,000 to the investor.

So a bond is essentially a formal IOU with a fixed schedule of repayment and interest.

Examples:

  • The US government issues Treasury bonds to fund public spending.
  • She invested her savings in corporate bonds to earn steady interest income.
  • The city issued bonds to raise money for building a new hospital.

Why is it called a "bond"? Because it binds the borrower legally to pay back the money as promised.

Key terms you'll hear with financial bonds:

  • Issuer — the one who creates and sells the bond (the borrower: a government, city, or company).
  • Bondholder — the person who buys the bond (the lender/investor).
  • Coupon rate — the interest rate paid to the bondholder.
  • Maturity — the date when the loan ends and the original money is paid back.
  • Face value / Par value — the original amount the bond is worth (e.g., $1,000).

In chemistry, a bond is the force that holds atoms together to form molecules. Atoms are the tiny building blocks of everything, and a chemical bond is what "glues" them to each other.

Examples:

  • Water (H₂O) exists because two hydrogen atoms are bonded to one oxygen atom.
  • The bond between atoms in a diamond is so strong that it makes diamond one of the hardest substances on Earth.

There are different types of chemical bonds (covalent, ionic, hydrogen, metallic), each describing how atoms share or transfer electrons to stick together — but the idea is always the same: a bond is the connection that holds atoms in place relative to each other.
5. Physical Bonds — Chains, Ropes, or Restraints

In an older and more literal sense, bonds (often used in the plural) refers to physical things that restrain or imprison someone — like chains, ropes, handcuffs, or shackles.

Examples:

  • The prisoner struggled to break free from his bonds.
  • She was held in bonds and couldn't escape.

This meaning is less common in everyday modern speech, but you'll encounter it frequently in literature, historical texts, and religious writings (e.g., "breaking the bonds of slavery").
6. An Adhesive Bond (in materials and construction)

When two surfaces stick together — because of glue, cement, heat, or another substance — the connection formed between them is called a bond.

Examples:

  • The glue created a strong bond between the two pieces of wood.
  • The weld formed a permanent bond between the metal parts.
  • A good primer improves the bond between paint and the wall.

Here, the word describes how well and how tightly two surfaces cling to each other.
7. A Surety Bond or Bail Bond (Legal)

In legal and insurance contexts, a bond is a formal financial guarantee that someone will fulfill an obligation — and if they don't, the person or company who issued the bond will pay the penalty.

  • A bail bond: When someone is arrested and the court sets a bail amount (say, $10,000), a bail bond is a guarantee (often provided by a bail bondsman) that the accused will show up for their court date. If the accused runs away, the bondsman pays the court.
  • A surety bond: A contractor might be required to hold a surety bond before starting a construction project. If they fail to complete the work as promised, the bond pays the client for the loss.

Think of it as a financial safety net backed by a promise.
8. A Bond in Bricklaying and Construction

In construction, a bond refers to the pattern or arrangement in which bricks, stones, or blocks are laid so that the joints between them are staggered. This staggering makes a wall much stronger.

Examples:

  • The mason used a running bond to build the garden wall (where each brick overlaps the one below it by half).
  • Different types of bonds — like the Flemish bond or English bond — create different patterns and strengths.

Even though "bond" has many different meanings across different fields, they all share the same soul: a connection that holds things together and carries a sense of obligation, strength, or commitment. Whether it's the love between two people, an atom holding to another, a legal contract, or a brick interlocked with its neighbor — a bond is what keeps things from falling apart.

Here's a quick mental map of all the meanings:

  • People → emotional closeness and loyalty
  • Promises → a commitment you are bound to keep
  • Finance → a formal loan with fixed repayment terms
  • Chemistry → the force holding atoms together
  • Restraints → chains or ropes that physically bind someone
  • Surfaces → the sticking together of materials
  • Legal/Insurance → a financial guarantee of performance
  • Construction → the pattern of laying bricks for strength
1983: To bond means to join or connect things — or people — so closely that they become firmly tied to each other. That connection can be physical (like glue holding two surfaces together), chemical (like atoms joining to form a substance), emotional (like two friends growing deeply close), or even legal and financial. The word always carries the same essential idea: two or more things come together and stay together.
Sense 1: To Form an Emotional Connection

This is the most common everyday use of the word. When people bond, they develop a warm, genuine, close relationship with one another — a connection that feels strong and lasting.

Examples:

  • She bonded with her college roommate on the very first night.
  • The team bonded during the difficult project they worked on together.
  • New parents often bond deeply with their baby in the first few weeks.

Notice two important patterns here:

"Bond with" someone — this tells you who you are connecting with.
He bonded with his grandfather over summers spent fishing.

"Bond over" something — this tells you what brought you together, the shared thing that created the connection.
The two strangers bonded over their love of old movies.

Bonding between people isn't forced or instant. It builds naturally through shared experiences, trust, vulnerability, or time spent together. You cannot make yourself bond with someone — it happens. This is why we say people "bond" rather than simply "become friends." Bonding suggests a deeper, more instinctive kind of closeness — the kind a mother feels with her child, or soldiers feel after going through hardship together.
Sense 2: To Stick or Join Physically

When a material, substance, or surface bonds, it sticks firmly and tightly to another surface — usually through an adhesive (like glue), heat, pressure, or a chemical reaction. The result is that the two things are held together and are difficult or impossible to separate.

Examples:

  • This industrial glue bonds metal to glass in under a minute.
  • The tiles have bonded permanently to the concrete floor.
  • The layers of the material bond when exposed to heat.

You'll notice "bond" can be used in two ways here:

Transitive (the glue does the bonding to something): The adhesive bonds the pieces together.

Intransitive (the materials bond on their own): The surfaces have bonded.

Both are correct and common.

In chemistry, atoms and molecules bond when they link together to form a new, larger structure. This happens when atoms share or exchange electrons. The result is a chemical compound — a completely new substance.

Examples:

  • Carbon atoms bond with hydrogen atoms to form hydrocarbons.
  • Oxygen and hydrogen bond to create water.
  • The atoms bond together through a process called covalent bonding.

This is a technical use, but it's the same idea — two things come together and stay together firmly.
Sense 4: To Guarantee or Secure (Legal/Financial Use)

This use is more formal and specialized, but worth knowing. In legal and financial contexts, to bond someone or something means to secure them through a guarantee — a kind of formal promise backed by money — that ensures they will fulfill their obligations honestly.

In practice, you'll most often see this in the past participle form: bonded.

Examples:

  • All our workers are fully bonded and insured. (meaning: their employer has taken out a financial guarantee covering any dishonest or harmful acts they might commit)
  • The contractor must be bonded before starting the job. (meaning: they must have a surety bond — a financial safety net for the client)

If a business says their staff are "bonded," they mean that if an employee steals from you or causes damage, there is a financial policy in place to cover your loss. It is a mark of trustworthiness and professional accountability.

Even across these very different uses, one thread runs through all of them: a bond is not a loose or casual connection. Whether it's glue holding two tiles together, atoms forming a molecule, two people growing close through shared experience, or a legal guarantee tying a contractor to their obligations — bonding always implies a connection that is strong, lasting, and not easily broken. The verb captures that quality of things being genuinely, firmly held together.
Common Collocations (Words That Often Appear with "Bond")

• bond with — connect emotionally with someone
  • bond over — connect because of a shared interest or experience
  • bond together — join as a unified group or mass
  • quickly bond / instantly bond — form a connection rapidly
  • bond to a surface — adhere physically
  • fully bonded — legally/financially guaranteed

When used emotionally, "bond" carries a sense of warmth and depth. To say two people "bonded" is to say something meaningful happened between them — not just that they got along, but that something genuine and lasting was built. This is why "bond" is often used when describing relationships under pressure or difficulty: soldiers, teammates, survivors, new parents. Those are the conditions where real bonds form.
1984:
Bonding means the process of forming a strong connection or union between two or more things — whether those things are people, atoms, materials, or legal/financial entities.

Think of it this way: wherever something is being joined together — physically, chemically, emotionally, or contractually — bonding is likely the right word to describe that process.
The Main Areas Where "Bonding" Is Used

"Bonding" is used in several distinct fields, and each has its own precise meaning. A truly well-rounded understanding of the word requires knowing all of them.

1. Emotional / Social Bonding

This is the meaning most people encounter first in everyday life.

Bonding here refers to the process of forming a deep emotional connection or attachment between people. It's not just liking someone — it's the gradual building of trust, closeness, and a sense of belonging with another person.

Key examples:

  • Parent-child bonding: When a mother holds her newborn immediately after birth, a powerful emotional attachment begins to form. This early bonding is considered critical for the child's psychological development.
  • Friendship bonding: Two people who go through a shared challenge — like surviving a difficult project at work or a long road trip — often feel closer afterward. Shared experiences accelerate bonding.
  • Team bonding: Companies organise team-bonding activities (games, retreats, group tasks) to help colleagues trust and work with each other better.
  • Romantic bonding: In relationships, bonding deepens over time through honest conversations, physical closeness, shared memories, and vulnerability.

The key point: Bonding is always a process, not a single moment. It builds over time and requires some form of meaningful interaction or shared experience.

2. Chemical Bonding

In chemistry, bonding refers to the forces or links that hold atoms together to form molecules or larger structures.

Everything around you — water, air, your body, a piece of plastic — exists because atoms are bonded to each other. Without bonding, matter as we know it simply would not exist.

There are several types of chemical bonding:

  • Ionic bonding: One atom gives an electron to another atom, and the resulting opposite electrical charges attract each other. Example: table salt (sodium and chlorine atoms bonded this way).
  • Covalent bonding: Two atoms share electrons between them. This is very common in nature. Example: water molecules (oxygen and hydrogen share electrons).
  • Metallic bonding: In metals, electrons flow freely among many atoms, holding the structure together. This is why metals conduct electricity and can be shaped easily.
  • Hydrogen bonding: A weaker type of bonding that occurs when a hydrogen atom is attracted to a highly electronegative atom (like oxygen or nitrogen) in a nearby molecule. Hydrogen bonding is why water has many of its unique properties — like surface tension and a high boiling point.

The key point: Chemical bonding explains why substances have the properties they do — their strength, melting point, conductivity, and reactivity all depend on the type of bonding present.

3. Physical / Material Bonding (Construction and Manufacturing)

Bonding in construction and manufacturing refers to the physical joining of materials together, either through an adhesive, heat, pressure, or a deliberate structural pattern.

Key examples:

  • Adhesive bonding: Gluing two surfaces together — like bonding tiles to a floor using tile adhesive, or bonding two pieces of metal using industrial epoxy. A bonding agent is any substance that helps two materials stick together.
  • Brick bonding: In bricklaying, "bonding" refers to the specific pattern in which bricks are laid so that each brick overlaps the joints of the bricks below it. This interlocking pattern gives a wall its strength. Common patterns include "stretcher bond" and "English bond."
  • Fabric bonding: In textiles, bonding is the process of fusing two layers of fabric together using heat, adhesive, or ultrasonic waves — creating a single, sturdier material.
  • Laminate bonding: In manufacturing, thin layers of material are bonded together to create a stronger composite — like in plywood or laminated glass.

The key point: In physical contexts, bonding always involves creating a union that is stronger than the individual parts alone.

4. Dental Bonding

Dental bonding is a cosmetic and restorative dental procedure in which a tooth-coloured resin material is applied to a tooth and hardened using a special light, permanently bonding it to the tooth's surface.

It is used to:

  • Repair chipped or cracked teeth
  • Improve the appearance of discoloured teeth
  • Close gaps between teeth
  • Change the shape of teeth
  • Protect exposed tooth roots when gums recede

The key point: The word "bonding" here is used in a physical sense — the resin material is literally bonded (chemically and physically attached) to the tooth structure.

5. Electrical Bonding

In electrical engineering and safety, bonding refers to the process of intentionally connecting multiple conductive (metal) parts of a structure or system with a conductor wire so that they are all at the same electrical potential (voltage level).

Why does this matter?

  • If two metal parts are at different electrical potentials and you touch both at the same time, electricity can flow through your body — causing a shock or even death.
  • Bonding ensures that no dangerous voltage difference exists between different metal parts.
  • It also helps prevent sparks, which is especially critical in environments where flammable gases or liquids are present (like fuel storage areas or aircraft refuelling stations).

Important distinction: Bonding is not the same as grounding (earthing), although they work together. Grounding connects the system to the earth to carry away fault current. Bonding equalises potential between the parts of the system itself.

The key point: Electrical bonding is fundamentally a safety measure — it prevents electric shock and sparks by ensuring everything conductive in a system is electrically connected.

6. Surety Bonding (Legal / Financial)

In law and finance, bonding (often called surety bonding) refers to a legally binding guarantee, backed by a third-party company (called a surety), that a person or business will fulfil a specific obligation or duty.

Think of it as a specialised form of insurance — but instead of protecting you from loss, a surety bond protects the other party (your client, employer, or the public) from loss caused by your failure to perform.

How it works:
There are three parties involved:

  • The Principal — the person or business that needs the bond (e.g., a contractor)
  • The Obligee — the party who requires the bond as protection (e.g., a government agency or a client)
  • The Surety — the bonding company that issues the bond and guarantees the principal's performance

If the principal fails to meet their obligations, the obligee can make a claim against the bond, and the surety will pay out — up to the bond's value.

Common uses of surety bonding:

  • Construction: A contractor must be bonded before they can work on a public building project. If they fail to complete the work, the bonding company compensates the client.
  • Employee bonding: Businesses that employ workers who handle cash or sensitive assets (like security guards or bank tellers) may require those employees to be bonded — protecting the business if the employee commits theft or fraud.
  • Court/legal bonds: A bail bond is a type of surety bond that guarantees an accused person will appear in court.
  • Licensing: Many professions (electricians, plumbers, financial advisors) are required by law to be bonded before they can legally operate.

The key point: In the financial/legal world, bonding is about accountability and protection — it creates a financial safety net for one party against the failure of another.
How All These Meanings Are Connected

Even though "bonding" is used in very different fields, there is one unifying idea running through every single meaning:

Bonding always involves creating a connection — one that provides strength, security, or trust.

  • Emotional bonding → trust and closeness between people
  • Chemical bonding → forces that hold atoms together and make substances stable
  • Physical bonding → joining materials for structural strength
  • Dental bonding → attaching material to a tooth for restoration
  • Electrical bonding → connecting parts to create safety
  • Surety bonding → a contractual connection that provides financial security

Emotional bonding — building deep relationships through shared experience and trust.

Chemical bonding — the forces that hold atoms together in molecules and compounds.

Physical bonding — joining materials (bricks, fabrics, metals) using adhesives, heat, or structural patterns.

Dental bonding — a procedure where resin is attached to a tooth to repair or improve it.

Electrical bonding — connecting conductive parts of a system so they are at equal voltage, preventing shock and sparks.

Surety bonding — a financial/legal guarantee by a third party that someone will fulfil their obligations.

Knowing all six of these will allow you to correctly understand and use the word "bonding" in virtually any context you encounter it — whether in a newspaper, a science textbook, a legal document, or an ordinary conversation.
1985:
A bone is one of the hard, rigid pieces that form the internal framework inside the body of a human or animal. All these bones together make up the skeleton — the structural "scaffolding" that holds your body up and gives it its shape.

Think of it this way: your body is like a building. The bones are the steel frame hidden inside — you can't see them, but without them, everything would collapse.

Bones are not just chunks of dead rock inside your body. They are living tissue — they grow, repair themselves when broken, and change throughout your life.

What they are made of:
A bone has two layers. The outer shell is dense and very hard — this is called compact bone. Beneath that is a spongy, lighter layer with tiny holes in it — called spongy bone (or cancellous bone). This design makes bones incredibly strong while keeping them light enough that you can move.

The main materials in bone are:

  • Calcium and phosphorus — minerals that give bone its hardness
  • Collagen — a tough protein that gives bone some flexibility so it can absorb shock without snapping

Inside most large bones, there is a hollow space filled with bone marrow — a soft, fatty substance. Marrow is surprisingly important: it is where your body produces red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets (the cells that help your blood clot when you get a cut).

On the outer surface of a bone is a very thin layer of tissue called the periosteum. This layer supplies blood to the bone and plays a role in healing when a bone breaks.

Bones carry out several essential jobs:

1. Support and structure
Without bones, you would be a shapeless blob of soft tissue. Your bones give your body its upright shape, hold your organs in place, and allow you to stand, sit, and move.

2. Protection
Some bones act like armour for your most vital organs:

  • The skull wraps around and protects the brain.
  • The ribcage (the curved cage of bones on your chest) shields your heart and lungs.
  • The vertebrae (the chain of bones running down your back, also called the spine or backbone) protect your spinal cord — the main nerve pathway of your body.

3. Movement
Muscles are attached to bones by tough cords called tendons. When a muscle contracts (shortens), it pulls the bone it is attached to, and that is how you move your arm, kick a ball, or turn your head.

4. Producing blood cells
As mentioned, the marrow inside bones constantly makes new blood cells — millions every second.

5. Storing minerals
Bones act as a mineral bank. When your body needs calcium (for nerve and muscle function, among other things), it can withdraw it from the bones. When you eat calcium-rich food, the bones store the extra.

An adult human body has 206 bones. Interestingly, babies are born with about 270–300 bones, but many of these small bones gradually fuse together as the child grows, reducing the total to 206 by adulthood.

Bones are connected to each other at places called joints (like your knee joint, elbow joint, or hip joint). The bones in a joint are held together by tough bands called ligaments.

Types of bones by shape:
Bones come in different shapes depending on the job they do.

  • Long bones — longer than they are wide. These make up the limbs. Examples: the femur (thighbone), the humerus (upper arm bone). They act as levers for movement.
  • Short bones — roughly cube-shaped, found in places that need stability and some movement. Examples: the small bones in your wrist and ankle.
  • Flat bones — thin and plate-like. Examples: the skull, ribs, shoulder blade. They protect organs and provide large surfaces for muscles to attach.
  • Irregular bones — complex, odd shapes that don't fit the other categories. Examples: the vertebrae of the spine, and many of the bones in your face.
  • Sesamoid bones — small bones embedded within a tendon, acting like a pulley. The most familiar example is the patella (kneecap).

Some of the most well-known bones:

  • Skull (cranium) — the dome of bone encasing the brain
  • Mandible — the lower jaw; the only movable bone in the skull
  • Clavicle — the collarbone, a slender bone connecting your shoulder to your chest
  • Sternum — the breastbone at the centre of your chest
  • Ribs — 12 pairs of curved bones forming the chest cage
  • Vertebrae — the 33 stacked bones of the spine
  • Pelvis — the basin-shaped group of bones at the hip
  • Femur — the thighbone; the longest and strongest bone in the human body
  • Patella — the kneecap
  • Tibia and fibula — the two bones of the lower leg
  • Humerus — the single bone of the upper arm
  • Radius and ulna — the two bones of the forearm
  • Carpals — eight small bones forming the wrist
  • Phalanges — the bones of the fingers and toes

When we say "a bone", we usually mean a single, individual bone inside a living body — or the physical remains of one after the animal has died.

When we say "bone" without an article (like "made of bone"), we treat it as a material — the hard, dense substance that bones are made of. Historically, people used the hard bones of animals to make tools, needles, handles for knives, and small objects. Even today, "bone" is used in the names of some materials:

  • Bone china — a type of very fine, translucent porcelain. It was originally made using ash from burned animal bones, which made it unusually white and strong.
  • Bone meal — ground-up bones used as a fertiliser in gardening.

"Bone" is also used to describe a colour — specifically, a pale, creamy off-white, like the colour of old or dried-out bone. It is a common name in interior design, fashion, and paint for a warm white that is not quite pure white.

Many common English words are built from the word "bone":

  • Backbone — literally, the spine. Figuratively (and very commonly), it means moral courage, determination, or strength of character. ("He has no backbone" means he is weak-willed or cowardly.)
  • Wishbone — the V-shaped bone (called the furcula) found in a bird's chest. By tradition, two people pull the two ends of a dried wishbone; whoever gets the larger piece gets to make a wish.
  • Jawbone — the jaw (typically the lower jaw).
  • Shinbone — the tibia, the prominent bone at the front of the lower leg.
  • Cheekbone — the prominent bone of the cheek (the zygomatic bone).
  • Collarbone — the clavicle.
  • Knucklebone — the bony knob at a finger joint.
  • Trombone — (borrowed from Italian; not related to "bone" in meaning, just in spelling.)
  • Fishbone — the small, sharp bone inside a fish.

The word "bone" appears in a large number of common English expressions. These are figurative — they don't literally refer to bones in the body.

"Have a bone to pick with someone"
To have a complaint or grievance you want to discuss with someone. ("I have a bone to pick with you — you forgot to call me back.")

"A bone of contention"
A specific issue or topic that is the source of an ongoing argument or disagreement between people. ("The division of the inheritance was a bone of contention in the family for years.")

"Make no bones about something"
To say something directly, honestly, and without hesitation or apology. ("She made no bones about the fact that she disliked his work.")

"Feel it in one's bones"
To have a strong inner feeling or intuition about something, even without clear evidence. ("I feel in my bones that something is wrong.")

"Throw someone a bone"
To give someone a small, token reward, concession, or favour — just enough to keep them satisfied, but not really enough to be truly helpful or generous. ("He didn't get the promotion, but they threw him a bone by giving him a small raise.")

"Bare bones"
The most basic, stripped-down, essential version of something — with nothing extra added. ("The bare bones of the plan are solid, but it needs a lot more detail.")

"Chilled to the bone" / "Frozen to the bone"
Feeling extremely cold — so cold that it feels as if even the bones inside you are cold. ("Standing in that blizzard, I was chilled to the bone.")

"Cut to the bone"
To reduce something as drastically as possible, to the absolute minimum. ("The budget cuts were so severe, they cut the team to the bone.")

"Work one's fingers to the bone"
To work extremely hard, to exhaustion. ("She worked her fingers to the bone to support her family.")

"Close to the bone" (also "near the bone")
Said of a remark or joke that is uncomfortably close to a painful truth, or that goes just far enough to be offensive. ("That joke about his divorce was a bit close to the bone.")

"Skin and bones" / "A bag of bones"
Said of a person or animal that is very thin, almost to the point of being unhealthy. ("The poor stray cat was just skin and bones when we found it.")

"In one's bones"
Deeply and naturally part of someone — something felt or known at the most fundamental level. ("She's an artist to her bones.")
"Bones" (plural) Used Informally for the Body Itself

In casual or slightly old-fashioned speech, "bones" (plural) can refer to the body as a whole, or the body's frame. ("Rest your weary bones" means rest your tired body. "His old bones ached in the cold" means his aging body ached in the cold.)

"Bones" also used to mean dice, historically, because dice were originally carved from the knucklebones of animals. This use is old and mostly found in literature or historical contexts.

"Bone" refers to the hard, living pieces of tissue that form the skeleton inside a vertebrate body. Bones support the body, protect organs, enable movement, produce blood cells, and store minerals. As a material, "bone" refers to the dense, pale substance these structures are made of — and has been used by humans throughout history as a raw material for tools and objects. As a colour, it means creamy off-white. And as part of everyday language, "bone" appears in dozens of common idioms and compound words, almost always carrying some echo of its core meaning: hardness, depth, fundamental structure, or the innermost part of something.
1986:
A "bone of contention" is a specific issue, topic, or matter that causes disagreement or argument between two or more people (or groups). It is the central point around which a conflict or dispute revolves.

Think of it as the exact thing two sides are fighting about — not the fight itself, but the subject at the heart of it.

For example, if two siblings constantly argue about who gets to use the family car, the car is the bone of contention. If two countries are in a long-standing dispute over a piece of land, that land is the bone of contention.

The phrase is centuries old and paints a vivid, simple picture in your mind. Imagine two dogs fighting over a single bone. Both want it. Neither will let go. The bone is the one thing causing all the growling and snapping between them.

This image was borrowed to describe human arguments. Just like the dogs and their bone, when two people or groups are locked in disagreement, the "bone" is the specific issue they are both pulling at from opposite sides.

The word "contention" comes from the Latin word contentio, which means struggle, rivalry, or dispute. So "bone of contention" literally and figuratively means "the bone over which there is a struggle."

The phrase has been in use in the English language since at least the 16th century, and it has remained in everyday use ever since — a sign of how perfectly the image captures the idea.

Bone — represents the specific issue, topic, or object at the center of the conflict. It's not just any issue; it's the one thing both sides want to "own" or resolve in their favor.

Contention — means disagreement, dispute, or argument. If something is "in contention," it is being argued over or competed for.

Put them together: a bone of contention = the specific thing being argued over.
How It Is Used in a Sentence

This phrase is a noun phrase, which means it functions as a "thing" in a sentence — it can be the subject, object, or complement of a sentence.

It almost always appears with the article "a" or "the":

  • "The division of household chores has long been a bone of contention between the two roommates."
  • "Salary increases became the bone of contention at the negotiating table."
  • "Land ownership is a major bone of contention in that region."
  • "How to spend the holiday budget turned out to be a bone of contention at the family dinner."
  • "Data privacy remains a bone of contention between tech companies and governments."

You can also use modifiers like "major," "real," "long-standing," or "constant" before it to show how serious or persistent the disagreement is — for example, "a real bone of contention" or "a long-standing bone of contention."
Key Things to Understand About This Phrase

It is neutral. The phrase does not take sides. It doesn't tell you who is right or wrong. It simply identifies the point of disagreement. You can use it to describe a conflict even if you are not personally involved.

It implies persistence. A bone of contention is usually not a one-off, five-second argument. It tends to suggest an issue that has caused repeated or ongoing conflict — something that keeps coming up and doesn't get resolved easily.

It can be used in any scale of conflict — from small personal disagreements (two friends arguing about money) to large political or international disputes (two nations disagreeing over a policy or territory).

It is both formal and informal. You can use this phrase in casual everyday conversation, in a professional email, in a news article, or in an academic essay. It fits all contexts naturally.
Don't Confuse It With "A Bone to Pick"

A very common phrase that sounds similar but means something different is "I have a bone to pick with you."

This means: "I have a specific complaint or grievance I want to raise with you." It is more personal and one-sided — one person is dissatisfied and wants to confront another.

A bone of contention, on the other hand, is the shared issue that both sides are disagreeing about. It's the subject of a two-way (or multi-way) dispute, not just one person's complaint.

Think of it this way: you might "have a bone to pick" with your colleague about something, and that something is the "bone of contention" between you two.

Several other phrases and words convey a similar meaning, and knowing them will help you recognize the idea when it appears in different forms:

"Point of contention" — essentially the same meaning as "bone of contention." Both are widely used, and you can often swap one for the other.

"Sticking point" — an issue that prevents two sides from reaching an agreement, often used in negotiations.

"Matter of dispute" or "subject of dispute" — more formal ways of saying the same thing.

"Apple of discord" — a more literary phrase borrowed from Greek mythology. In the story, a golden apple caused a fierce argument among goddesses, ultimately leading to the Trojan War. Like "bone of contention," it refers to something that sparks conflict, but "apple of discord" sounds more dramatic and literary.

"Contentious issue" — an adjective form; a "contentious issue" is an issue that causes contention, which is essentially the same idea from a different angle.
A Quick Summary to Lock It In

A bone of contention is the specific subject, issue, or matter that lies at the heart of a disagreement between people or groups. The image is simple: two dogs fighting over one bone. The bone is what they're fighting over, not the fight itself. In human terms, whenever two sides are arguing, whatever they're arguing about is the bone of contention. It's a neutral, versatile, and timeless phrase used across all kinds of contexts — personal, professional, and political — to point clearly to the root cause of a conflict.
1987:
When someone says "I have a bone to pick with you," it means they are unhappy about something you did or said, and they want to talk about it, discuss it, or sort it out. They have a complaint, a disagreement, or a grievance — and they want to address it directly with you.

Think of it as the person saying: "There is something bothering me, and it involves you. We need to talk."
Where does this expression come from?

The image behind this idiom comes from a dog chewing on a bone.

When a dog gets a bone, it doesn't let go easily. It gnaws at it, works at it, and keeps coming back to it until it's done. The bone demands the dog's full attention — it's a problem the dog keeps working at, over and over.

In the same way, when a person has "a bone to pick" with someone, they have a problem they can't just ignore and walk away from. It's something they need to chew on, work through, and resolve. The expression has been in use in English since at least the 16th century, and this core image — of persistent, determined attention to something — has stayed the same.

The most common structure is:

"I have a bone to pick with you."

But it can also appear as:

"We need to talk — I have a bone to pick with you."
"She had a bone to pick with her manager."
"Do you have a bone to pick with me?"

Notice that "bone to pick" almost always comes with a person attached — "with you," "with him," "with her." That's because this idiom is about a conflict or grievance between two specific people. You pick a bone with someone, not just generally.
The tone: serious, but not aggressive

This is important. "A bone to pick" sits in the middle ground — it's not a casual thing, but it's also not a threat or a declaration of war.

It implies:

  • There is a real issue that needs to be addressed.
  • The person is unhappy or annoyed.
  • They want a conversation or a resolution — not just to vent or fight.

If someone says "I have a bone to pick with you," the right response is to take them seriously and hear them out. It's an invitation to resolve something.

A few things to be clear about:

  • It does not mean the person wants a physical fight. It's about a conversation, not a confrontation.
  • It does not mean the issue is tiny and unimportant — but it also doesn't mean the world is ending. It could be anything from "you didn't tell me the meeting was moved" to "you've been spreading false things about me."
  • The size of the grievance depends entirely on the situation and tone. The idiom itself is neutral about how big or small the problem is.

1. At work:

"Hey, before the meeting — I have a bone to pick with you. You took credit for my idea in front of the whole team."

  1. Between friends:

"I need to pick a bone with you. You told everyone about my surprise party!"

  1. In a lighter, joking way:

"I have a bone to pick with you — you ate the last piece of cake and didn't tell me!"
(Here, the tone makes it clear it's playful, not a serious complaint.)

  1. Formal writing or reporting:

"The senator has a bone to pick with the new policy, arguing it undermines local governance."

"A bone to pick" is an informal expression. You'll hear it most in:

  • Everyday spoken conversation
  • Casual writing (texts, emails between friends)
  • News and journalism (in a slightly informal tone)

You would generally avoid it in:

  • Formal business letters
  • Academic writing
  • Official legal or diplomatic language

In those settings, you'd replace it with something like: "I have a concern I'd like to raise," or "I wish to address a grievance."

While "I have a bone to pick with you" is the standard form, you might also see:

  • "a few bones to pick" — meaning the person has multiple complaints, not just one.
  • "pick a bone with someone" — same meaning, slightly restructured.

Both are natural and mean the same thing at heart.

Core meaningI have a complaint or disagreement I want to discuss with you
OriginA dog persistently chewing a bone — the image of working through something that demands attention
ToneSerious but not aggressive; invites resolution
FormalityInformal / conversational
Used withAlways directed at a specific person: "with you / him / her / them"

In short: if someone says "I have a bone to pick with you," brace yourself for a calm but frank conversation about something you did that upset or bothered them. It's their way of saying, "I'm not going to let this go until we sort it out."

Bonhomie means a warm, easy, cheerful friendliness — the quality of being genuinely good-natured in a way that makes everyone around you feel comfortable and welcome.

Think of someone you know who always seems relaxed and pleasant to be around. Not someone who is putting on a performance of being nice, and not someone who is loud and over-the-top, but someone who has a natural, easy warmth that makes any room feel a little lighter the moment they walk in. They smile easily, they make you feel at ease, they are never stiff or cold, and conversations with them flow without effort. That quality — that genuine, sunny, open good-naturedness — is exactly what bonhomie means.

The word is a noun, so it describes a quality or a state. A person can have bonhomie, they can radiate bonhomie, or a social gathering can be full of bonhomie.
What makes bonhomie special — and different from just "friendliness"?

"Friendly" is a fairly flat word. A shop assistant can be friendly. A customer service email can be written in a friendly tone. But bonhomie is richer than that. It carries three things at once:

Warmth — It is genuinely felt, not performed. It comes from inside a person, not from obligation.

Cheerfulness — There is a lightness and good humor to it. A person with bonhomie tends to be pleasantly upbeat and easy to laugh with.

Ease — It is effortless and relaxed. There is nothing strained, nervous, or try-hard about it.

Together, these three things create something more specific than simple friendliness. Bonhomie is the kind of quality that makes people say things like, "He just has a way about him," or "She makes everyone feel instantly at ease."
How it differs from similar words:

Charisma is about magnetic, compelling personal power that draws people toward you — it can even be a little intimidating. Bonhomie is softer and warmer. A charismatic person commands attention; a bonhomous person makes you feel at home.

Joviality is about being jolly, merry, and full of laughter — it leans heavily on the cheerful side. Bonhomie includes that cheerfulness, but it is also warmer and more genuine. Joviality can sometimes feel like a performance; bonhomie almost never does.

Affability means being easy to approach and talk to — it is the closest cousin of bonhomie. But affability is more passive (you are easy to talk to), while bonhomie is more active and alive (you actively radiate warmth and good cheer).
Where you'll see this word used:

Bonhomie is a slightly elevated, literary word. You won't hear it much in casual everyday conversation, but you will see it often in books, journalism, and formal writing when the writer wants to describe someone's personality with precision. If a writer uses this word, they are specifically reaching for that combination of warmth, good humor, and ease — nothing else quite captures it.

"The host greeted every guest with such genuine bonhomie that even the shyest people in the room quickly felt at ease."

"He was well-liked not for his intelligence or his success, but for his natural bonhomie — an openness that made strangers feel like old friends within minutes."

"The small café had a warm atmosphere of bonhomie, with regulars chatting freely across tables as though they had known each other for years."

Notice that in the last example, bonhomie describes not a person but a social atmosphere — the feeling in a room. This is a common and completely correct use of the word. A place, a gathering, or a moment can be full of bonhomie when the warmth and friendliness of the people in it create a shared, cheerful ease.

Bonhomie is the genuine, warm, cheerful, effortless good-naturedness that some people have — and sometimes some places have — that makes everyone around feel comfortable, welcome, and happy to be there.
1989:
Bonkers is an informal adjective that means crazy, wildly irrational, or completely absurd. It is the kind of word you use when something or someone has gone so far beyond normal, reasonable, or sane behaviour that ordinary words like "strange" or "odd" just don't feel strong enough.

Think of it as a step well past "weird" and firmly into "this makes no sense at all."
The Three Main Ways It Is Used

1. To describe a person who is acting crazy or irrational

When you call a person bonkers, you mean they are behaving in a way that is wild, unhinged, or completely unreasonable — as if they have lost their grip on logic or reality.

"My neighbour woke up at 3 AM to mow his lawn. The man is absolutely bonkers."

"She spent her entire salary on lottery tickets. Has she gone bonkers?"

"Don't listen to him — he's bonkers."

Important note: Bonkers is not a clinical or medical word. You would never use it in a doctor's report or to seriously describe someone with a mental illness. It is casual, everyday language — and it usually carries a tone of disbelief or humour, not cruelty.

2. To describe a situation, idea, plan, or event that is absurd or hard to believe

This is perhaps the most common use today. When a situation is bonkers, it means it is so strange, outrageous, or unbelievable that it feels disconnected from reality. The person using the word is expressing genuine shock or disbelief.

"Did you hear what happened at the meeting? The whole thing was completely bonkers."

"They want us to finish a 6-month project in two weeks. That's bonkers."

"The plot of that film is bonkers — I couldn't follow any of it."

"He said he'd fix the roof by jumping off it. Bonkers idea."

Here, bonkers is not about a person being mentally unstable — it is simply a strong way of saying: "This is absurd. This makes no sense. This is beyond what a reasonable person would expect."

3. To describe wild excitement or enthusiasm (especially in "go bonkers")

The phrase go bonkers is very commonly used to describe someone — or a crowd — that reacts to something with extreme, uncontrolled excitement or enthusiasm. The "craziness" here is positive and energetic, not negative.

"The crowd went absolutely bonkers when the band walked on stage."

"My dog goes bonkers every time he sees his leash."

"She went bonkers when she heard she'd won the prize."

In this sense, bonkers simply means to lose control with excitement or joy. It is not negative at all.
Register and Tone: When and How People Use It

Bonkers is informal and colloquial. This means:

  • You would say it in casual conversation with friends, family, or colleagues you are comfortable with.
  • You would not write it in a formal essay, a business report, a legal document, or an academic paper.
  • It is perfectly appropriate in everyday speech, social media, journalism (informal pieces), and light-hearted writing.

The tone of bonkers is almost always one of the following:

  • Humorous — laughing at how ridiculous something is
  • Exasperated — frustrated by how irrational something or someone is
  • Amazed — genuinely shocked that something so absurd is real
  • Enthusiastic — when used with "go bonkers," it's warm and energetic

It is rarely used to genuinely insult someone in a deeply offensive way. It's more like a raised eyebrow in word form.
Degree: How Strong Is the Word?

Bonkers implies a high degree of craziness or absurdity. It is not a mild word. If you call something bonkers, you are not saying it is slightly odd — you are saying it is remarkably, noticeably, hard-to-ignore crazy or absurd.

It is often made even stronger with intensifiers:

"completely bonkers," "absolutely bonkers," "totally bonkers," "utterly bonkers"

All of these just push the meaning further — even more crazy, even more absurd.

• It is not a formal or medical diagnosis. Never use it in place of words like "mentally ill" or "psychotic" when speaking seriously about health.
  • It is not deeply offensive like some other insults, but in a sensitive context (talking about someone's genuine mental health struggles), it is better to avoid it — it can feel dismissive.
  • It is not a mild word. Don't use it for something that is just slightly unusual. Reserve it for things that are genuinely over-the-top.

Understanding bonkers is easier when you see it alongside words of similar meaning:

  • Crazy — the most common equivalent; bonkers is just more colourful and British-sounding.
  • Mad — very close in meaning (especially in British English).
  • Insane — similar, but slightly more intense and can be used more seriously.
  • Nuts — informal, very similar to bonkers.
  • Absurd — similar when describing situations, but more formal.
  • Ridiculous — similar, but focuses on something being laughably unreasonable.

Bonkers sits comfortably among these as a lively, expressive, and slightly playful choice.

MeaningCrazy, irrational, absurd, or wildly excited
Used forPeople, situations, ideas, events, reactions
ToneHumorous, exasperated, amazed, or enthusiastic
RegisterInformal/casual only
DegreeStrong — implies a lot of craziness or absurdity

In short: if you witness something that makes you think "this is so crazy it barely feels real" — that is your bonkers moment.
